chapter_theme: Seven songs at Tiruppandanainallur (திருப்பந்தணை நல்லூர்): courtesans of the street who ask first whether a man has money, the poet's mala and deeds, and pleas for the jnana teaching, the feet, the gift of rhythmic Tamil, and for remembering Murugan even in pleasure; the praise names the goddess as Sivai, Sambhavi and Parai, bindu and sound.
structure_note: Courtesan songs (850, 852, 853, 854, 856); a chant of Murugan's names (851); and 855, which promises to hold Murugan's feet and arms in mind even while sporting with women.

850.reading: The poet describes the courtesans of the street, scented with sandal and civet, cloud-haired, cuckoo-voiced, walking like peacocks with anklets ringing and lisping like parrots, whose first thought is 'is there money?', who change the minds and deeds of those who see them, and asks Murugan to end the sorrow of the maya of these deceivers who sleep by day and some nights. The praise, in drum syllables, shows the battle with Sura's army and the birds and jackals feeding, names the goddess Sivai, Sundari, Sambhavi and Parai, Siva's left half, as his mother, and Murugan with Valli and Devayanai as the pure guru of Pandanai.
850.nuance: பணம் உண்டென தவலம்படு நினைவு: the women's thought turns at once to money, the mark of the price-woman. The goddess's names (சிவை, சுந்தரி, சம்பவி, பரை) are a litany of Sakti; the song gives them to Murugan's mother.

851.reading: The poet asks that his two deeds fear, coming deeds plead, the dark disease sleep and mala and maya fade, that Murugan's grace swell, and that, singing his lofty praise and calling 'moon-faced Muruga, Kadamba, son of Siva, Kandha, Guha, Vela' and 'Siva Siva' with a clear heart, he be given the dancing anklets. The praise names the nephew of Vishnu who took the life of the marutha trees and Kamsa, the hero on the golden peacock who circles the demons' hill, the son loved by the pure Lord who rides the bull with his consort, and the lord of Pandanai with his two consorts.
851.nuance: The plea is a string of names, a chant within the song; சிவசிவ என்று தெளிவுறு நெஞ்சு makes the clarity of heart come through repeating Siva's name. The first lines personify deeds and disease: past deeds fear, coming deeds beg.

852.reading: The poet describes the price-women who shame swans in gait, play dramas, sing, run up debts, fall for anyone with great show of passion and cast the net of deceit, and asks that he, a dog of a servant who fell into infatuation and gained passion, disease and illness, wander no more but be given the nectar of mantra and jnana teaching and the anklets, so that grace enters when he calls 'Muruga' with love. The praise names the vel that burned seas and islands, Siva clothed in elephant and tiger skin who took the poet as his servant, Sadasiva whose side Uma never leaves, Vishnu who bears Lakshmi on his chest, and Valli's lord at Pandanai.
852.nuance: அமுத மந்திர ஞானோபதேசமும் அருளி: the plea is for initiation, a mantra given as teaching. கரி நெடும் புலி தோல் உடையார் எனை அடிமை கொண்ட சுவாமி: the poet calls Siva the one who made him his servant, a rare first-person claim on the father rather than the son.

853.reading: The poet speaks of women with pot-like breasts and parrot speech, musk in their hair, with whom he stirs up mischief and gives friendship, and asks not to wither in hell but to be given the mind to worship the feet that came round Kailasa. The praise names Murugan son of the goddess who shares half of the river-bearer, born of her old tapas, dweller at cloud-wrapped Pandanai, lord even to Sankara who came down under the jambu tree's shade, who ended the fear of the gods.
853.nuance: சம்பு நிழலுக்குள் வந்து அவதரித்த சங்கரர் points to Siva under the jambu tree, the form worshipped at Thiruvanaikka, and Murugan is called lord even to him. வண்கயிலை சுற்றி வந்திடு பதம may recall Murugan circling the world or Kailasa, but the allusion is unclear.

854.reading: The poet tells how fish-eyed women with flowered hair coax him to bed, scent him with powder and embrace him with sweet words, and asks that the sorrow of that infatuation end through the fragrant lotus feet, with thandai, kinkini and anklets ringing, coming always to him so that his cruel deeds, anxiety and mala perish. The praise names Murugan to whom devotees cry 'refuge', who wed Devayanai and the Kurava girl, whose vel crushed the arms of the gods' enemies, and Saravana at Pandanai among monkeys, champak, agil, sandal and konrai.
854.nuance: The ringing of the anklets is sung in sound (கலின் கலின், கிணின் கிணின்), the feet arriving audibly; the plea is that they come to him (வந்திரும்), not that he go to them.

855.reading: The poet lists the beauty of women from honey lips and crystal smile to lotus feet, and says that even if he plays in sorrow in the pleasure of union with them, he will lovingly hold in his heart Murugan's lotus feet, his twelve arms and his chest with its garland. The praise names his mother as the Siva-form of 'Om Namah', five-faced, Neeli, Kalyani, the light of bindu and the dwelling of sound, Abhirami Ambika; Murugan whose vel made the demons' blood run while gandharvas sang, the lover of Valli and Devayanai, the lord of Pandanai where Siva wears karanthai, konrai, the moon and the river.
855.nuance: The song does not ask to leave the women: விளையாடினும் ... பரிவுளங்கொள்வேனே, 'even if I play, I will hold you in mind', makes remembrance the vow, as in 153. The mother's names ஓநமந்த சிவரூபி ... விந்து ஒளி ஓசை தங்கும் make the goddess bindu and nada, the Tirumanthiram's terms.

856.reading: The poet speaks of women with moon faces and parrot voices, like Menaka and Rati, like sea-goddesses, who stay daily in the street while men bring wealth and gold jewels and go, and asks not to wander under their sway but, with wealth abundant through many tapas, to know the wisdom of speaking of Murugan and to pour out rhythmic Tamil fit to sing him. The praise names Siva of the spreading matted hair who rejoiced in Uma's worship, the city that flourishes on a river equal to the nine Gangas, Murugan who blessed the ganas, gods, Hari, Brahma, Mukunda and the poets, and the vel that split Krauncha.
856.nuance: நிகர் சந்தத் தமிழ் சொரிந்து பாட: the gift asked is the rhythmic Tamil of the Thiruppugazh itself. நதிபங்கில் ... கந்துகாபுரி, the name of the city by the river, is unclear.

links.note: Both promise to keep Murugan in mind even while sunk in women's pleasure; 153 says he will never forget, 855 names what he will hold, the feet, the twelve arms and the chest.
